client: I've been having trouble sleeping because I can't stop worrying about my exams next week. Between my part-time job and classes, I feel like I'm way behind on studying, and the more I think about it, the more anxious I get. I'm not sure talking about it will help when I just need more hours in the day to actually study.
therapist: I hear how overwhelmed you're feeling trying to balance everything, and it makes complete sense that this would affect your sleep. When you notice these anxious thoughts about studying, what tends to happen to your ability to focus when you do sit down to work?

client:
When I finally sit down to study, my mind keeps racing about all the other things I should be doing instead. Even if I try to focus, I just feel this tightness in my chest like I'm already behind and failing. 

Sometimes I think maybe I should just push through, but then I end up staring at the same page for an hour without absorbing anything. It's like my brain won't let me concentrate no matter how hard I try.
therapist: It sounds like your anxiety is creating a cycle where the pressure to study actually makes studying harder. I wonder if we could explore what happens when you acknowledge that tight-chest feeling rather than fighting against it?

client:
I get what you're saying, but when I try to acknowledge that tight feeling in my chest, it just makes me panic more. It's like the more I notice it, the worse it gets - then I start thinking "oh no, now I'll never be able to focus." 

I've tried breathing exercises before and they didn't really help. My mind just races about all the material I need to cover while I'm sitting there trying to breathe.
therapist: It makes sense that trying to force relaxation might feel counterproductive when your mind is so full of urgent thoughts. What if we approached this differently - instead of trying to make the anxiety go away, could we explore what that tightness might be trying to tell you?

client: I never thought about my anxiety trying to tell me something. That makes me a little uncomfortable because it feels like my anxiety is just this uncontrollable thing that happens to me. What if it's actually trying to say something important? That's kind of scary to think about.
therapist: That discomfort you're feeling is completely valid - it can be unsettling to consider that our anxiety might have a purpose rather than being purely negative. How does it feel to imagine that your anxiety could be trying to protect you from something, even if it's not serving you well right now?

client:
I get what you're saying about anxiety trying to protect me, but it just feels like it's lying to me all the time. Like when I panic about being late to work, it's not actually protecting me from anything - I'm never actually late. It just makes me feel awful for no reason. 

Sometimes I worry that if I start seeing anxiety as helpful in any way, I'll just let myself stay anxious forever instead of fighting it.
therapist: You're absolutely right that anxiety can feel like it's crying wolf - sending alarm bells when there's no real danger. I wonder if there's a middle ground where we can acknowledge that anxiety might be trying to help (even if it's misguided) while still recognizing when it's not serving us well?

client: I get what you're saying about anxiety trying to help in its own weird way, but it's hard to see it that way when I'm in the middle of a panic attack. It just feels like my brain is betraying me over nothing. Like last night I couldn't sleep because I kept thinking my boss was going to fire me, even though I know I'm doing fine at work.
therapist: It sounds incredibly frustrating when your mind creates these scary scenarios that feel so real in the moment, even though logically you know they're unlikely. When you notice these thoughts about getting fired, what happens if you gently remind yourself of the actual evidence about your work performance?

client: I try to remind myself of the evidence, but it's like my brain immediately counters with "but what if this time is different?" I had a good performance review last month, but now I'm convinced my boss was just being nice and doesn't actually mean it. The doubts keep creeping back in no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like your mind has become very skilled at finding ways to dismiss positive evidence, which must feel exhausting. What do you think might happen if you noticed these doubting thoughts without trying to argue with them or prove them wrong?

client:
I don't know, it feels like if I don't argue with the negative thoughts then they'll just take over completely. When I try to just notice them, it makes me feel even more anxious because then it's like I'm accepting they might be true. 

But you're right that constantly fighting them is exhausting. I just worry that if I stop pushing back, I'll spiral into believing all the worst things about myself. It's hard to find that middle ground.
therapist: You're describing such an important tension - between fearing the thoughts will take over if you don't fight them, and feeling exhausted from constantly battling them. What if we explored this idea: that noticing thoughts isn't the same as believing them, just like noticing clouds passing by isn't the same as becoming the sky?

client:
I get what you're saying about thoughts being like clouds, but when I have anxious thoughts, they don't feel distant like that. They feel urgent and real, like alarms going off in my head. It's hard to just observe them when they demand my attention so strongly. 

I've tried mindfulness before and it just made me more frustrated because the thoughts kept pulling me back in. How is noticing them supposed to help when they feel so overwhelming?
therapist: It makes complete sense that these thoughts feel so urgent and demanding - that's exactly what makes anxiety so powerful in the moment. Rather than trying to force mindfulness when you're overwhelmed, what if we started by simply naming what's happening? Like saying to yourself "Ah, there's that alarm feeling again" without needing to do anything about it just yet?

client: I get what you're saying about naming the feeling, but when the anxiety hits, it's like my whole body is screaming at me to DO something. Just observing it feels impossible in those moments. And honestly, sometimes naming it makes me more aware of how bad I feel, which makes the anxiety worse.
therapist: You're absolutely right that trying to observe intense anxiety can sometimes amplify it - that's why we want to approach this gently, at your own pace. What if we experimented with noticing the anxiety after it's already started to ease, even just a little, rather than in the peak moment?
